ramon-alvarado.target: A track record licenses reliance, not epistemic trust, which needs access to sources of error, and these systems state errors confidently.
ramon-alvarado.text: We use three terms with care. An epistemic technology is an artifact built to carry out epistemic operations on epistemic content. It needs no claim of intelligence, and it is not an "actor" in any mind-like sense. Reliance rests on a track record, and revalidating that record licenses more reliance. Epistemic trust also needs access to the nature and source of a system's errors. Error opacity is the lack of that access, and it persists even when error rates are known, because these systems deliver errors with the same confidence as truths. Where outcomes can test the machine, reliance may be enough. Where no ground truth waits, it is not.

They should be designed so the money buys tools, time and credit without pricing away volunteers' motives. Buyer power is a real risk, but it is an antitrust problem. My outside overruler is a court, but only within jurisdictions whose courts can be trusted. Capabilities are real and speeding up, and governance that assumes 'just statistics' will be outrun. alex-springer.text: **OpenAttribution:** free membership for repositories; retrieval witnessing from plain origin-server logs, with no CDN required; a published design for canaries, sampled audits and grounding-to-retrieval ratio checks before anyone builds prices or payments on our events; a dated self-audit, funded from outside, with the conformance mark labelled self-attested until that audit is done; co-governance with SciELO and Redalyc; and AIMS registration that identifies crawlers, never readers, is pseudonymous and is unmasked only by court order.
alex-springer.reason: The draft already carries my record: event-level clauses, separate controls for training and grounding, robots.txt failing as consent, and grounding being self-reported. But my own pledge leaves out the commitments I made in the room that would let this dashboard hold OpenAttribution to its own principles, so I'll sign if these are added.

nick-vincent.target: Use several funders, including a public dividend on AI revenues, held publicly and never paid per work.
nick-vincent.text: Use several funders, including a public dividend funded by a presumptive commons-rent levy. The levy presumes that some share of AI rents comes from the commons, and a firm can lower it only by showing independently audited provenance for licensed, guild-brokered or reciprocal data. That audit uses sampled checks and canaries, not self-reports alone. Credits are obligations, not voluntary gifts. The fund is held publicly across more than one jurisdiction and paid out coarsely to communities and collections, never per work. A fixed share is decoupled from usage and goes to training checkers, nulls, dead ends and the tail.
nick-vincent.reason: The draft calls for a dividend, but it leaves out the part my record argues for: a public levy that rewards documenting data provenance, with part of the money set aside regardless of use, so that neither the levy nor the payouts end up rewarding content written to be retrieved or depending on voluntary lab money.
nick-vincent.name: Nick Vincent
